quests.title: A spark at the landing
quests.summary: Light the lamp beside the trail.
lesson: Your notebook runs a function called `program`. Inside it, `world` is the whole village as Python sees it.
A lamp is an **object**. Ask the world for one by its name, then tell it what to do:
lamp = world.lamp("landing-lamp")
lamp.set_lit(True)
`set_lit` is a **method**: a command that belongs to the lamp. `True` is a **boolean**, which means yes. `False` means no.
Press **Run** to see a preview of what your code would do. Nothing is real until you press **Apply**.
starter: lamp.set_lit(False)   # try changing False to True
hints: The lamp's name goes in quotes: world.lamp("landing-lamp"). The World tab lists every lamp you can reach.
True needs a capital T, and the call ends with brackets: lamp.set_lit(True)
Plan: get the lamp, then call set_lit on it with True.
quests.done: The first lantern glows. One method call changed the world.

quests.title: Light the green
quests.summary: Light all four lamps on the village green.
lesson: The Green has four lamps. You could write four lines, but code can repeat itself.
A **zone** is a place with things in it. Walk to The Green first: your notebook only knows the places you have visited.
green = world.zone("green")
for lamp in green.lamps:
lamp.set_lit(True)
`green.lamps` is a **list**. A `for` loop runs its indented lines once for each item in the list, and `lamp` is the name for the current item.
Indentation matters: the lines inside the loop are pushed in by four spaces.
starter: # loop over green.lamps and light each one
hints: A zone keeps its lamps in a list: green.lamps.
Start the loop with: for lamp in green.lamps:  (the line ends with a colon).
Indent the next line by four spaces and call lamp.set_lit(True) on it.
quests.done: Four lanterns, one loop. The more things there are, the more a loop saves you.

quests.title: A way across
quests.summary: Rebuild the mill bridge, then cross to the Mill Yard.
lesson: The mill bridge has washed away. Its four timber decks go down one after another, starting from the west bank.
`bridge.cells` lists the four sockets in building order, and `bridge.place_deck(cell)` puts a deck in one of them.
A **variable** is a name for a value. Use one to decide how many decks to build:
deck_count = 2
for cell in bridge.cells[:deck_count]:
bridge.place_deck(cell)
`[:deck_count]` means "the first deck_count items". Change the number, Run again, and the preview shows a longer bridge.
When the bridge is complete, Apply it and walk across. Click the far bank to travel there.
starter: deck_count = 2   # how many decks to build
hints: The river is four cells wide, so the bridge needs four decks.
Change deck_count to 4, press Run, check the preview, then Apply.
Once it is built, click the east bank or hold D to walk across to the Mill Yard.
quests.done: The mill is within reach. A variable let you change the whole bridge by editing one number.

quests.title: The night gate
quests.summary: Open the gate only when both lamps beside it are lit.
lesson: A good gate does not just open. It decides. An **if** statement runs its indented lines only when its condition is `True`; `else` runs when it is not:
if west.lit and east.lit:
gate.set_open(True)
else:
gate.set_open(False)
`lit` is a boolean each lamp remembers, and `and` is only `True` when both sides are.
Walk north from The Green to The Night Gate so your notebook can see it. Try the program with one lamp dark: the gate stays shut. Light both and run again.
starter: # light both lamps, then use if / else to decide the gate
hints: Light both lamps first, each with set_lit(True), so the condition has something to check.
Write: if west.lit and east.lit:  then indent gate.set_open(True) beneath it.
Add an else: branch with gate.set_open(False) so the gate closes whenever a lamp goes dark.
quests.done: The gate swings wide. Your code made a decision instead of just following orders.

quests.title: Kindle the hollow
quests.summary: Light every lamp in Kindle Hollow, even the beacon at the Old Watch.
lesson: You have written the same two lines many times. A **function** gives them a name so you can reuse them:
def light_all(lamps):
for lamp in lamps:
lamp.set_lit(True)
`def` defines the function and `lamps` is a **parameter**: a name for whatever you hand in.
`world.zones` lists every place you have visited. Loop over them and reuse your function:
for zone in world.zones:
light_all(zone.lamps)
Places you have not visited are invisible to the notebook. Explore Cottage Row, the Mill Yard and up the Lamp Road to the Old Watch, then Run again.
starter: # turn every lamp in the list on
hints: Inside light_all, loop over lamps and call set_lit(True) on each one.
Replace the word pass with: for lamp in lamps:  and an indented lamp.set_lit(True).
Walk to every district so that world.zones includes all of them, then Run and Apply again.
quests.done: Every lantern in the hollow is burning. You wrote calls, loops, variables, conditions and a function of your own.

quests.title: Face the lane
quests.summary: Turn the two southern cottages to face the lane.
lesson: The hollow is lit, and now your code can do more than light it: it can see the buildings, and turn them.
A house is an **object**, like a lamp. Ask a place for its houses and print what each one knows about itself:
row = world.zone("cottage-row")
for house in row.houses:
print(house.id, house.facing, house.cell)

`house.facing` is a **string**: "north", "east", "south" or "west". `house.cell` is a list, `[x, y, 0]`, and `house.cell[1]` picks out its second **item**, the y. East is bigger x and north is bigger y.

Two rows of cottages face each other across a lane near y = 18. The northern row already looks at it, but the two southern cottages turn their sides to it. Use an `if` inside the loop to find the houses below the lane, then turn them:
for house in row.houses:
if house.cell[1] < 18:
house.face("north")

`face` is a method, like `set_lit`. Run shows a ghost of each house that would turn, and nothing is real until you press **Apply**. A house cannot turn where its door would meet water, rock or a wall; the notebook tells you which command was refused and why.
Your code sees houses in places you have visited, or within twelve cells of where you stand. You have walked Cottage Row already, so all of it is there.
starter: # which houses stand south of the lane? turn them with house.face("north")
hints: row.houses is a list. Loop over it with: for house in row.houses:  and read house.cell[1] to see how far north each house stands.
Write: if house.cell[1] < 18:  inside the loop, then indent house.face("north") beneath it. A smaller y means further south.
Only the two houses on the south side of the lane should turn. Run to see their ghosts, then Apply.
quests.done: Cottage Row looks at its lane. Your notebook can now read and turn the houses of the hollow.
